- No handler implements the drop-dims flatten; `as.double()`/`as.integer()`
  each hand-roll their own cast and return early on an already-correct mode,
  which is what preserves the logical matrix's dims.
- The `matrix()` handler extracts the arguments it knows and ignores the
  rest, while `array()` validates its argument set.
- `check_assignment_compatible()` returns early when *either* side passes as
  a scalar, which was meant only to let a rank-0 value into a `double(1)`
  target but exempts every scalar/array pairing along with it.
- The `diag()` handler and `infer_dest_diag()` both gate the identity form
  on `x@rank == 0L` where R gates on `length(x) == 1L`.

## Expected behavior

- Nested masked reductions compile: one mask hoister per reduction context,
  whatever the nesting.
- Reassignment applies the same per-axis conformability policy the rest of
  the compiler uses: a statically wrong extent is a compile error, a
  symbolic one is a runtime guard. Scalar right-hand sides (which broadcast)
  and deferred-shape `NA`-dim locals keep working as they do today.
- A BLAS/LAPACK destination is reused in place only when its rank and every
  extent are *proven* equal to the result's; anything else goes through a
  temporary and is copied under the reassignment check above.
- `declare(type(x = double))` says the dimensions are missing; a
  non-atomic mode is named in the error instead of reaching the code
  generator.
- `c(<matrix>)` and `as.vector()` flatten column-major and drop dims,
  matching R, and `as.integer()`/`as.double()` of a matrix do the same.
- `matrix(dimnames = )` is refused at compile time, as `array()` is.
- Reassignment between a scalar and an array shape is refused in both
  directions, with the exemption narrowed to the case it was for (both
  sides length 1).
- `diag(x)` follows R's `length(x) == 1` rule, so `diag(n)` with a declared
  `integer(1)` is the n-by-n identity, and the size is `as.integer(x)` as in
  R — meaning a `double` or `logical` `x` works and truncates toward zero.
  That needs `as.integer()` to be spellable in a size expression.

title: Using `quickr` in a package requires importing it
declare(parallel()) can generate incorrect results for scalar accumulation loops
description:
## Summary
`declare(parallel())` can emit an OpenMP loop with a shared scalar accumulator update (`total <- total + x[i]`), which is a data race and produces incorrect/nondeterministic results.

Original report and discussion: https://github.com/t-kalinowski/quickr/pull/88#issuecomment-3817079544

## Verified on
- Branch: `main`
- Local reproduction date: 2026-02-17

## Minimal reproducible example
```r
library(devtools)
load_all(quiet = TRUE)

loop_sum_unsafe <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = double(n)))
  total <- 0.0
  declare(parallel())
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    total <- total + x[i]
  }
  total
}

Sys.setenv(OMP_NUM_THREADS = "4", OMP_THREAD_LIMIT = "4", OMP_DYNAMIC = "false")
q_unsafe <- quick(loop_sum_unsafe)

x <- rep(1, 100000L)
vapply(1:6, function(i) q_unsafe(x), numeric(1))
```

### Expected
Each run should return `100000`.

### Observed
Repeated calls return incorrect and varying results (example from local run):
`30961, 31102, 25000, 31544, 30804, 31507`

## Generated code shape
`r2f(loop_sum_unsafe)` emits:
```fortran
!$omp parallel do
do i = 1, size(x)
  total = (total + x(i))
end do
!$omp end parallel do
```

This loop updates shared `total` without a reduction/private strategy.

## Notes
`declare(parallel(private = total))` is not currently accepted on `main` (`parallel() does not accept arguments yet.`), so users cannot express a reduction/private fix in the current interface.

title: Feature: Matrix operations.
description:
It is possible to link/connect to the BLAS/LAPACK that R is using. This allows us to translate matrix multiplication (`%*%`) to a fortran call to `dgemm` from the linked BLAS. 

I believe we can implement more or less all base R matrix operation in quickr. 

I have in cooperation with codex created a branch that works as a proof-of-concept; [mns-nordicals/quickr/tree/matrix](https://github.com/mns-nordicals/quickr/tree/matrix). I have also changed the readme to kind of get an overview of R to BLAS translation.  

The next question is; is there any meaning to doing this as we will call the same BLAS implementation as base R? I have created this benchmark of a linear regression that is inspired by the example from [RcppArmadillo](https://github.com/RcppCore/RcppArmadillo) which is used by over 1200 packages on cran. 

```r
devtools::load_all()

Rcpp::sourceCpp(
  code = '#include <RcppArmadillo/Lighter>
// [[Rcpp::depends(RcppArmadillo)]]

// [[Rcpp::export]]
Rcpp::List fastLm(const arma::mat& X, const arma::colvec& y) {
    int n = X.n_rows, k = X.n_cols;

    arma::colvec coef = arma::solve(X, y);     // fit model y ~ X
    arma::colvec res  = y - X*coef;            // residuals
    double s2 = arma::dot(res, res) / (n - k); // std.errors of coefficients
    arma::colvec std_err = arma::sqrt(s2 * arma::diagvec(arma::pinv(arma::trans(X)*X)));

    return Rcpp::List::create(Rcpp::Named("coefficients") = coef,
                              Rcpp::Named("stderr")       = std_err,
                              Rcpp::Named("df.residual")  = n - k);
}'
)

my_lm <- function(X, y) {
  declare(type(X = double(n, k)), type(y = double(n)))
  n <- nrow(X)
  k <- ncol(X)

  XtX <- crossprod(X)
  Xty <- crossprod(X, y)
  coef <- solve(XtX, Xty)

  res <- y - X %*% coef
  s2 <- crossprod(res) / (n - k)

  U <- chol(XtX)
  XtX_inv <- chol2inv(U)

  std_err <- sqrt(diag(XtX_inv) * s2)
  df <- n - k

  list(
    coefficients = coef,
    stderr       = std_err,
    df.residual  = df
  )
}

q_my_lm <- quick(my_lm)

X <- cbind(1, matrix(rnorm(3 * 10^6), ncol = 3))
beta <- c(0.5, 1.0, -2.0, 3)
y <- as.vector(X %*% beta + rnorm(nrow(X), sd = 2))

bench::mark(
  my_lm(X, y),
  q_my_lm(X, y),
  fastLm(X, y),
  lm(y ~ X[, -1]),
  min_iterations = 100,
  check = FALSE
)[c(1:5, 7, 9)]

# A tibble: 4 × 7
  expression           min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc n_itr total_time
  <bch:expr>      <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt> <int>   <bch:tm>
1 my_lm(X, y)       18.3 ms   21.9 ms     43.5     7.63 MB   100       2.3 s
2 q_my_lm(X, y)     10.3 ms   10.5 ms     93.9         0 B   100      1.06 s
3 fastLm(X, y)      58.4 ms     61 ms     15.8         0 B   100      6.33 s
4 lm(y ~ X[, -1])  199.3 ms  245.9 ms      3.89   294.1 MB   100     25.73 s
```

I am on fedora 42 which as uses openBLAS and all my cores. We see that the fortran version is twice as fast as the base R. I don't know if the comparison to RcppArmadillo is fair, but as far as I can see it should also be linked to the same BLAS as R. 

The generated fortran code is a bit ugly ... codex thinks it is safer to create a bunch of tmp variables. 

```fortran
subroutine my_lm(X, y, coef, std_err, df, X__dim_1_, X__dim_2_) bind(c)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_int
  implicit none

  ! manifest start
  ! sizes
  integer(c_int), intent(in), value :: X__dim_1_
  integer(c_int), intent(in), value :: X__dim_2_

  ! args
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: X(X__dim_1_, X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: y(X__dim_1_)
  real(c_double), intent(out) :: coef(X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double), intent(out) :: std_err(min(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_))
  integer(c_int), intent(out) :: df

  ! locals
  real(c_double) :: XtX_inv(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp11_
  real(c_double) :: s2
  integer(c_int) :: k
  real(c_double) :: tmp9_(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  integer(c_int) :: n
  real(c_double) :: Xty(X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double) :: XtX(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double) :: tmp7_(X__dim_1_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp16_
  integer(c_int) :: tmp5_(X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double) :: res(X__dim_1_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp14_
  real(c_double) :: tmp3_(X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double) :: U(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp12_
  real(c_double) :: tmp1_(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp10_
  real(c_double) :: tmp8_
  integer(c_int) :: tmp17_
  integer(c_int) :: tmp6_
  real(c_double) :: tmp4_(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  integer(c_int) :: tmp15_
  real(c_double) :: tmp13_(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_)
  real(c_double) :: tmp2_(X__dim_2_)
  ! manifest end


  n = size(X, 1)
  k = size(X, 2)
  call dgemm('T','N', X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_, X__dim_1_, 1.0_c_double, X, X__dim_1_, X, X__dim_1_, 0.0_c_double, tmp1_, X__dim_2_)
  XtX = tmp1_
  call dgemv('T', X__dim_1_, X__dim_2_, 1.0_c_double, X, X__dim_1_, y, 1, 0.0_c_double, tmp2_, 1)
  Xty = tmp2_
  tmp4_ = XtX
  tmp3_ = Xty
  call dgesv(X__dim_2_, 1, tmp4_, X__dim_2_, tmp5_, tmp3_, X__dim_2_, tmp6_)
  coef = tmp3_
  call dgemv('N', X__dim_1_, X__dim_2_, 1.0_c_double, X, X__dim_1_, coef, 1, 0.0_c_double, tmp7_, 1)
  res = (y - tmp7_)
  tmp8_ = dot_product(res, res)
  s2 = (tmp8_ / real((n - k), kind=c_double))
  tmp9_ = XtX
  call dpotrf('U', X__dim_2_, tmp9_, X__dim_2_, tmp10_)
  do tmp12_ = 1, X__dim_2_
    do tmp11_ = tmp12_+1, X__dim_2_
      tmp9_(tmp11_, tmp12_) = 0.0_c_double
    end do
  end do
  U = tmp9_
  tmp13_ = U
  call dpotri('U', X__dim_2_, tmp13_, X__dim_2_, tmp14_)
  do tmp16_ = 1, X__dim_2_
    do tmp15_ = tmp16_+1, X__dim_2_
      tmp13_(tmp15_, tmp16_) = tmp13_(tmp16_, tmp15_)
    end do
  end do
  XtX_inv = tmp13_
  std_err = sqrt(([(XtX_inv(tmp17_, tmp17_), tmp17_ = 1, min(X__dim_2_, X__dim_2_))] * s2))
  df = (n - k)
end subroutine
```

What do you think ? Is it worth it to implement it in quickr? I believe you know linear algebra much better than I - so consider this just a PoC. But if you are interested I could try to break it down into multiple PRs. 

It would likely add a lot of new code to r2f. Have you considered to use something like [box](https://github.com/klmr/box) or [dir](https://github.com/cynkra/dir) to organize the code into folders?

title: Gaurd agaisnt unassigned expressions / "empty" expression
description:
I think we need to check that all expressions are assigned to a symbol except for the last expression, which we already handle.

Consider this example;

``` r
add_one <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = double(n)))
  x = x + 1
  x + 1
  x
}
```

Which generates this code:

``` fortran
subroutine add_one(x, x__len_) bind(c)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_ptrdiff_t
  implicit none

  ! manifest start
  ! sizes
  integer(c_ptrdiff_t), intent(in), value :: x__len_

  ! args
  real(c_double), intent(in out) :: x(x__len_)
  ! manifest end


  x = (x + 1.0_c_double)
  (x + 1.0_c_double)
end subroutine
```

This create a compile error

```
Compiler Error: Unclassifiable statement at (1)
make: *** [/usr/lib64/R/etc/Makeconf:229: add_one_fsub.o] Error 1
---
Compiler exit status: 1 
```

because of   `(x + 1.0_c_double)`. 

A perhaps clearer example is


``` r 
return_x <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = double(n)))
  x
  x
}
```

Which also has the same compile error.

title: Use Mojo as the backend
description:
Currently, quickr transpiles R to Fortran. Switching the backend from Fortran to Mojo should be straightforward. The subset of Fortran that quickr targets is mostly covered by Mojo, including vectorized operations on arrays, reduction intrinsics, and slicing operators. Mojo also supports manifest-style forward variable declarations, similar to Fortran.

Mojo's SIMD capabilities seem stronger than Fortran's, and it already supports ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation:  
- https://docs.modular.com/mojo/manual/types#scalar-values
- https://docs.modular.com/mojo/faq/#is-mojo-interpreted-or-compiled  

Moving to Mojo could open a pathway for supporting autodiff in compiled R functions. Over time, it may also make it easier to leverage accelerators like GPUs and TPUs.  

It's still unclear whether this should be a new backend within quickr or a separate package with a fun name like `rojo` or `moarjo`.

Here is what codex had to say: 

# Unary handler Variable reuse causes compile-time error

Summary: Reusing the operand’s `Variable` object in unary handlers (e.g., `!`, unary `+`/`-`, and `abs`) carries identity fields like `@name`, `@is_arg`, and `@r` into the anonymous result. This can mark a local result as “external” and trigger external-argument casting logic later, producing invalid Fortran and a compiler error.


Reproduction
- Minimal function that negates a logical input into a local and uses it as a mask:

```r
devtools::load_all(quiet = TRUE)

qfun <- quick(function(x){
  declare(type(x = logical(NA)))
  y <- !x
  out <- ifelse(y, 1L, 0L)
  out
}, name = "bug_unary_not_local_cast")

qfun(c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE))
```

- Compiler error (gfortran):

```text
bug_unary_not_local_cast_fsub.f90:19:33:

   19 |   out = merge(1_c_int, 0_c_int, (y/=0))
      |                                 1
Compiler Error: Operands of comparison operator ‘/=’ at (1) are LOGICAL(4)/INTEGER(4)
```


What was generated and why it’s wrong
- The symbol emission logic converts external logicals to a boolean via integer compare:
  - `R/r2f.R:90` emits `(s/=0)` when a logical symbol is marked external (`@is_external`, i.e., arg/return).

- The unary not handler returns the operand’s `Variable` as-is:
  - `R/r2f.R:743`–`R/r2f.R:750` uses `Fortran(glue("(.not. {x})"), x@value)`.

- Assignment of `y <- !x` binds a new symbol using that same `Variable` instance:
  - `R/r2f.R:867`–`R/r2f.R:901` (new-symbol case) does `var <- value@value; var@name <- name; scope[[name]] <- var`.

- Because `x@value` had `@is_arg == TRUE` (it’s an input argument), the new local `y` inherits `@is_arg == TRUE` via reuse. That makes `y` look external, so when `y` appears later as a symbol, the symbol logic emits `(y/=0)`. But `y` is a local logical (not an integer), hence the invalid LOGICAL/INTEGER comparison seen in the compiler error.


Where the pattern appears
- Unary logical not:
  - `R/r2f.R:743`–`R/r2f.R:750`
- Unary plus/minus:
  - `R/r2f.R:660`–`R/r2f.R:669` (+)
  - `R/r2f.R:671`–`R/r2f.R:680` (-)
- abs (two definitions):
  - `R/r2f.R:542`–`R/r2f.R:546`
  - `R/r2f.R:586`–`R/r2f.R:593` (complex → double)
- Other unary elementals (sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sqrt, exp, log, floor, ceiling) also forward `arg@value`:
  - `R/r2f.R:552`–`R/r2f.R:572`


Root cause
- Reusing `arg@value` for anonymous unary results forwards identity fields (`@name`, `@is_arg`, `@is_return`, and `@r`).
- The symbol emission special-case for external logicals applies incorrectly to locals that have inherited `@is_arg`.


Fix
- In all unary handlers, create a fresh `Variable` for the result with the correct mode and dims, rather than forwarding `arg@value`:
  - Use `Variable(arg@value@mode, arg@value@dims)` (or appropriate mode override) and pass that as the Fortran value.
  - This avoids inheriting `@name`, `@is_arg`, and `@r`.

Concrete changes
- Logical not:
  - `R/r2f.R:743`–`R/r2f.R:750`
  - Replace:
    ```r
    Fortran(glue("(.not. {x})"), x@value)
    ```
    With:
    ```r
    Fortran(glue("(.not. {x})"), Variable("logical", x@value@dims))
    ```

- Unary plus/minus:
  - `R/r2f.R:660`–`R/r2f.R:669`, `R/r2f.R:671`–`R/r2f.R:680`
  - Replace `..., x@value)` with `..., Variable(x@value@mode, x@value@dims))`.

- abs (both places):
  - `R/r2f.R:542`–`R/r2f.R:546`: replace `arg@value` with `Variable(arg@value@mode, arg@value@dims)`.
  - `R/r2f.R:586`–`R/r2f.R:593`: for complex input, return `Variable("double", arg@value@dims)`; otherwise same as above.

- Other unary elementals (sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, sqrt, exp, log, floor, ceiling):
  - `R/r2f.R:552`–`R/r2f.R:572`: replace `arg@value` with `Variable(arg@value@mode, arg@value@dims)`.

Optional helper
- To keep code concise, introduce a small helper:
  ```r
  new_unary_value <- function(v, mode = v@mode) Variable(mode, v@dims)
  ```
  Then use `new_unary_value(arg@value)` or `new_unary_value(arg@value, "double")` where needed.


Evidence tests
- All current tests pass (`testthat::test_local()`), but the failing case above isn’t covered. A targeted test would catch regressions:
  - “logical arg; local y <- !x; then ifelse(y, 1L, 0L) compiles and runs.”


Key code references
- Symbol handling that casts external logicals: `R/r2f.R:90`
- Unary handlers forwarding `arg@value`:
  - `R/r2f.R:660`, `R/r2f.R:671`, `R/r2f.R:743`, `R/r2f.R:542`, `R/r2f.R:586`, `R/r2f.R:552`


TL;DR
- The pattern of returning `Fortran(..., arg@value)` in unary handlers makes locals inherit input-argument identity and triggers external-only casts, yielding invalid comparisons in generated Fortran. Constructing a fresh `Variable(mode, dims)` for unary results fixes the issue.

title: bug: unary "+", "-" and "!"
description:
I have come across some missing feature / bugs around unary operators (!, +, -)

Consider these three examples:

```r
fn <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = integer(n)))
  lgl <- x > 1L
  not_lgl <- !lgl
  not_lgl
}
qfn <- quick(fn)


fn <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = integer(n)))
  y <- -x
  y
}
qfn <- quick(fn)


fn <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = integer(n)))
  y <- +x
  y
}
qfn <- quick(fn)
```

The first fails because `!` is not implemented and unary `-` and `+` fail because they expect to be used in a binary context.

title: Add ability to return multiple values
description:
It would be nice to be able to return multiple values. 

Consider this toy example of an rle function created as mostly as a quickr function. 

```r
rle_combined <- function(x) {
  declare(
    type(x = integer(n)),
    type(lengths = integer(n)),
    type(values = integer(n))
  )
  
  n <- length(x)
  
  lengths <- 0L
  placeholder_value <- max(x) + 1L # placeholder
  values <- placeholder_value
  
  run_idx <- 1L
  run_length <- 1L
  values[1L] <- x[1L]  # First run value
  
  for (i in 2:n) {
    if (x[i] == x[i-1]) {
      run_length <- run_length + 1L
    } else {
      lengths[run_idx] <- run_length
      run_idx <- run_idx + 1L
      run_length <- 1L
      values[run_idx] <- x[i]
    }
  }
  # last run
  lengths[run_idx] <- run_length
  
  list(lengths = lengths, values = values, placeholder = placeholder_value)
}
```

Then we can use the returned values to recreate `base::rle`

```r
q_rle_combined <- quick(rle_combined)

my_rle<- function(x){
  combined_list <- q_rle_combined(x)

  out <- list(
    lengths = combined_list$lengths[combined_list$lengths > 0],
    values = combined_list$values[combined_list$values != combined_list$placeholder]
  )
  
  class(out) <- "rle"
  out
}
```

title: Bug in division operator "/"
description:
There is some subtle bug in the "/"-handler and perhaps in the conform function. I provide here my analysis. 

Consider this code

```r
my_mean <- function(x) {
  declare(type(x = double(NA)))
  mu <- sum(x) / length(x)
  mu
}

q_my_mean <- quickr::quick(my_mean)

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 8)

my_mean(x) # returns: 5.75
q_my_mean(x) # returns 5
```
The problem in this concrete example is that mu is created as an integer - and therefore 5.75 gets cast to 5

```Fortran
subroutine my_mean(x, mu, x__len_) bind(c)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_int, c_ptrdiff_t
  implicit none

  ! manifest start
  ! sizes
  integer(c_ptrdiff_t), intent(in), value :: x__len_

  ! args
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: x(x__len_)
  integer(c_int), intent(out) :: mu
  ! manifest end


  mu = (sum(x) / size(x))
end subroutine
```

The problem arises from the conform function. In this case sum(x) returns a scalar double and length(x) return a scalar integer. As neither is a vector/array they both fall though the conform function and the last variable determines the output container which is integer in this case. 

```r
conform <- function(..., mode = NULL) {
  var <- NULL
  # technically, types are implicit promoted, but we'll let <- handle that.
  for (var in drop_nulls(list(...))) {
    if (passes_as_scalar(var)) {
      next
    } else {
      break
    }
  }
  if (is.null(var))
    NULL
  else
    Variable(mode %||% var@mode, var@dims)
 }

```
A partial fix to this problem would be to set the mode in the conform call in the r2f handler.

```r
r2f_handlers[["/"]] <- function(args, scope = NULL, ...) {
  .[left, right] <- lapply(args, r2f, scope, ...)
  Fortran(glue("({left} / {right})"), conform(left@value, right@value, mode = "double")) # added mode = ...
}
```
But this only fixes this particular problem. If both a and b is declared as integers then a/b will be integer division in fortran and we will get the wrong result, but the right output type / container. 

Another problem would be if a and b were complex then the result would be down casted to a real. 

So I don't know if "/"-handler should be changed to check types or if there should be some changes to conform() for better type inference. 

There are some work around from the user side that fixes this, like declaring n as double and assign length to that first and use that in the calculation or declaring mu as a scalar double. That at least fixes this particular example of calculating the mean.

title: Error in value[[i]] : subscript out of bounds
description:
I am using `quickr` and `dotty` versions 0.1.0. Not sure if this is my fault, a problem in `quickr`, a problem in `dotty`, or something else entirely, but consider:

```r
slow_func <- function(x) {
   declare({
      type(x = integer(n))
      type(len = integer(n))
   })

   n <- length(x)
   y <- x[-1L] != x[-n]
   i <- c(which(y | is.na(y)), n)
   
   lens <- diff(c(0L, i))
   vals <- x[i]

   nv <- length(vals)
   lis <- vector("list", length = nv)
   for (j in seq_len(nv)) {
      lis[[j]] <- if (vals[j] == 0L) rep(0L, lens[j]) else seq_len(lens[j])
   }
   len <- unlist(lis)

   len
}
```

Some toy data for the sake of illustration:
```r
set.seed(6593)
x <- sample(c(-1L, 0L, 1L), size = 100L, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.4, 0.2, 0.4))
```

However this gives an error:

I am using R version 4.5.1 on Windows 11 x64. I also tested it under Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS (using R version 4.4.0) and got the same result.

title: Feature request: support for calling registered quickr functions from other quickr functions
description:
Sometimes it might be helpful to breakdown the problem into smaller sub problems/function. 

I imagine an api where you first create the sub-function in R and when called with `quick()` you can also choose to register as a sub-module. If it compiles and the function works on its own, then in the main function you can now call the sub-function. 

I imagine something like this:

```r
library(quickr)

# Define a reusable normalization function
normalize_vector <- quick(function(x) {
  declare(type(x = double(n)))
  norm <- sqrt(sum(x * x))
  x / norm
}, register_as_submodule = TRUE)

# Use it in a main computation
compute_cosine_similarity <- quick(function(a, b) {
  declare(type(a = double(n)), 
          type(b = double(n)))
  
  a_norm <- normalize_vector(a)  # Call to registered quickr function
  b_norm <- normalize_vector(b)  # Reuse the same function
  similarity <- sum(a_norm * b_norm)
  similarity
})
```

Then the generated Fortran code could look something like this:

```Fortran
module quickr_functions
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_int
  implicit none
  
contains
  
  subroutine normalize_vector(x, result, n) bind(c)
    real(c_double), intent(in) :: x(n)
    real(c_double), intent(out) :: result(n)
    integer(c_int), intent(in), value :: n
    real(c_double) :: norm
    
    norm = sqrt(sum(x * x))
    result = x / norm
  end subroutine
  
  subroutine compute_cosine_similarity(a, b, similarity, n) bind(c)
    real(c_double), intent(in) :: a(n), b(n)
    real(c_double), intent(out) :: similarity
    integer(c_int), intent(in), value :: n
    real(c_double) :: a_norm(n), b_norm(n)
    
    call normalize_vector(a, a_norm, n)
    call normalize_vector(b, b_norm, n)
    similarity = sum(a_norm * b_norm)
  end subroutine
  
end module 
```
I think there are several ways this could be implemented, interfaces, modules or just a collection of sub modules. This specific example was created with an LLM. 

Some weeks ago I tried to basically "vibe code" this with an LLM and got it to work. But honesty after many iterations I lost track of what had changed to the quickr package - I think it made many more changes than necessary. 

If this is within scope of quickr and you have some guidance, I would like to try to make it work - though I would note I am not experienced and would use an LLM.

title: `if` return value
`for` loop semantics differ slightly
description:
In a Fortran `DO` loop, the index is bumped once more after the last iteration, so it finishes at `end + step`. An R for loop leaves the index at the value that was used in the final iteration.

``` r
library(quickr)

fn <- function(n) {
  declare(type(n = integer(1)))
  for (i in seq(1, n)) NULL
  i
}

fn(5L)
#> [1] 5
quick(fn)(5L)
#> [1] 6
```

title: Logical comparison outside if()
description:
It might be nice to assign a name to a logical comparison. Take this example where I want to test if a or b is strictly greater than the other, but the difference is not more than 3

```
logical_test <- function(a, b) {
  declare(
    type(a = double(1)),
    type(b = double(1))
  )

  delta <- a - b
  if(delta < 0) {
    delta <- (-1) * delta
  } 

  a_gt_b <- a > b
  b_gt_a <- b > a
  delta_lt_3 <- delta <= 3

  out <- (a_gt_b || b_gt_a) && delta
  out
}
```
This gives a compile error as the code gets translates to  Fortran ( using quickr:::r2f() )

```
subroutine logical_test(a, b, out) bind(c)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_int
  implicit none

  ! manifest start
  ! args
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: a
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: b
  integer(c_int), intent(out) :: out ! logical

  ! locals
  logical :: b_gt_a ! logical
  real(c_double) :: delta
  logical :: a_gt_b ! logical
  logical :: delta_lt_3 ! logical
  ! manifest end


  delta = (a - b)
  if ((delta < 0.0_c_double)) then
    delta = (-1.0_c_double * delta)
  end if
  a_gt_b = (a > b)
  b_gt_a = (b > a)
  delta_lt_3 = (delta <= 3.0_c_double)
  out = a_gt_b/=0 .or. b_gt_a/=0 .and. delta_lt_3/=0
end subroutine
```
The problem seems to be  when we compare the logical variables at the end a "/=0" is added on.  Here is the compile error

> q_logical_test <- quick(logical_test)
> using C compiler: ‘gcc (GCC) 15.1.1 20250425 (Red Hat 15.1.1-1)’
> using Fortran compiler: ‘GNU Fortran (GCC) 15.1.1 20250425 (Red Hat 15.1.1-1)’
> gfortran  -fpic  -g -O2  -c  logical_test_fsub.f90 -o logical_test_fsub.o
> logical_test_fsub.f90:26:38:
> 
>    26 |   out = a_gt_b/=0 .or. b_gt_a/=0 .and. delta_lt_3/=0
>       |                                      1
> Error: Operands of comparison operator ‘/=’ at (1) are LOGICAL(4)/INTEGER(4)
> logical_test_fsub.f90:26:22:
> 
>    26 |   out = a_gt_b/=0 .or. b_gt_a/=0 .and. delta_lt_3/=0
>       |                      1
> Error: Operands of comparison operator ‘/=’ at (1) are LOGICAL(4)/INTEGER(4)
> logical_test_fsub.f90:26:8:
> 
>    26 |   out = a_gt_b/=0 .or. b_gt_a/=0 .and. delta_lt_3/=0
>       |        1
> Error: Operands of comparison operator ‘/=’ at (1) are LOGICAL(4)/INTEGER(4)
> make: *** [/opt/R/4.5.0/lib/R/etc/Makeconf:229: logical_test_fsub.o] Error 1

There is a work around by doing all the work in the if-statement like so

```
logical_test_2 <- function(a, b) {
  declare(
    type(a = double(1)),
    type(b = double(1))
  )

  delta <- a - b
  if(delta < 0) {
    delta <- (-1) * delta
  } 

  out <- (a > b ||  b > a) && delta <= 3
  out
}
```

This creates this fotran code

```
subroutine logical_test_2(a, b, out) bind(c)
  use iso_c_binding, only: c_double, c_int
  implicit none

  ! manifest start
  ! args
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: a
  real(c_double), intent(in) :: b
  integer(c_int), intent(out) :: out ! logical

  ! locals
  real(c_double) :: delta
  ! manifest end


  delta = (a - b)
  if ((delta < 0.0_c_double)) then
    delta = (-1.0_c_double * delta)
  end if
  out = (a > b) .or. (b > a) .and. (delta <= 3.0_c_double)
end subroutine
```

Here we see that "/=0" does not get tagged on and the code compiles and works.

title: Another benchmark
description:
This isn't an issue, but I would just like to say I think this package looks very interesting and I hope it get developed further.  I think it has a great potential to speed up many small and large functions that are written in pure R. If this issue is not relevant feel free to close / delete.

To test it for myself, I tried to see if one of my solution to Advent of Code 2024 could be sped up with quickr. 

I tried problem 2 part 1, where we have 1,000 sequences that we need to check that they are monotonically increasing or decreasing and that there is no jump greater than 3 between two adjacent numbers.  

My benchmark show that the quickr code runs 200 times faster than my original solution. In order to work within the constraints of quickr I had to re-write the code in R (which turned out to be faster than my original code). Compared to the re-written code quickr is 100 times faster. 

Even just checking one sub sequence of length 5-8 the quickr code is 5 times faster.

## benchmark

```
# A tibble: 5 × 7
  expression                   min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec` n_itr
  <bch:expr>              <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl> <int>
1 original                  4.84ms   5.02ms      194.   11.81KB     18.3    85
2 check_sub_seq             3.73ms   3.86ms      259.   11.81KB     23.5    99
3 check_all_sub_seq         2.41ms   2.46ms      406.    3.96KB     19.8   185
4 quick_check_sub_seq     728.34µs  742.7µs     1336.   11.81KB     23.9   614
5 quick_check_all_sub_seq   22.5µs  23.71µs    42053.        0B      0   10000
```
## code
Assuming the data / text input to the problem is in "txt_input.txt"

```
library(quickr)
library(stringr)
library(purrr)

## Data
sub_seq_list <- 
  readLines("txt_input.txt") |> 
  str_split("\\\n") |> 
  unlist() |> 
  str_split(" ") |> 
  map(as.integer)

all_seq_vec <- unlist(sub_seq_list)
sub_seq_idx <- cumsum(lengths(sub_seq_list))

## Original implimentation
org_check_sub_seq <- function(sub_sequence) {
  len_sequence <- length(sub_sequence)
  all_rising <- all_falling <- vector("logical", len_sequence - 1)
  delta <- vector("integer", len_sequence - 1)
  
  for (i in 2:len_sequence) {
    all_rising[i-1] <- sub_sequence[i-1] < sub_sequence[i]
    all_falling[i-1] <- sub_sequence[i-1] > sub_sequence[i]
    delta[i-1] <- abs(sub_sequence[i-1] - sub_sequence[i])
  }
  
  no_jumps <- all(delta <= 3)
  monotonicity <- all(all_rising) || all(all_falling)
  
  return(monotonicity && no_jumps)
}

## New implimentation to fit quickr
check_sub_seq <- function(sub_sequence) {
  declare(
    type(sub_sequence = integer(NA))
  )

  len_sequence <- length(sub_sequence)
  len_sequence_1 <- len_sequence - 1L
  out <- 0L

  # Indicator for condition
  rising <- 0L
  falling <- 0L
  no_jump <- 0L
  
  # count conditions
  rising_counter <- 0L
  falling_counter <- 0L
  jump_counter <- 0L

  for (left_idx in 1:len_sequence_1 ) {
    right_idx <- left_idx + 1L
    
    if(sub_sequence[left_idx] < sub_sequence[right_idx]) {
      rising_counter <- rising_counter + 1L
    }
    
    if(sub_sequence[left_idx] > sub_sequence[right_idx]) {
      falling_counter <- falling_counter + 1L
    }
    
    delta <- sub_sequence[left_idx] - sub_sequence[right_idx]

    if(delta < 0L) {
      delta <- delta * (-1L)
    }
    
    if(delta < 1L | delta > 3L) {
      jump_counter <- jump_counter + 1L
    }
  }

  # Check conditions
  if(rising_counter == len_sequence_1) rising <- 1L
  if(falling_counter == len_sequence_1) falling <- 1L
  if(jump_counter == 0L) no_jump <- 1L
  if(rising + falling + no_jump == 2L) out <- 1L
  
  out
}

## Check all sequcence in Fortran - not jumping back and forth between R
check_all_sub_seq <- function(all_sequences, sub_seq_idx) {
  declare(
    type(all_sequences = integer(NA)),
    type(sub_seq_idx = integer(NA))
  )
  
  out <- 0L
  endpoints <- c(0L, sub_seq_idx)
  
  for(subset_idx in 2:length(endpoints)) {
    left_endpoint <- endpoints[subset_idx - 1L] + 1L
    right_endpoint <- endpoints[subset_idx]
    sub_sequence <- all_sequences[left_endpoint:right_endpoint]

    len_sequence <- length(sub_sequence)
    len_sequence_1 <- len_sequence - 1L
  
    # Indicator for condition
    rising <- 0L
    falling <- 0L
    no_jump <- 0L
    
    # count conditions
    rising_counter <- 0L
    falling_counter <- 0L
    jump_counter <- 0L
  
    for (left_idx in 1:len_sequence_1 ) {
      right_idx <- left_idx + 1L
      
      if(sub_sequence[left_idx] < sub_sequence[right_idx]) {
        rising_counter <- rising_counter + 1L
      }
      
      if(sub_sequence[left_idx] > sub_sequence[right_idx]) {
        falling_counter <- falling_counter + 1L
      }
      
      delta <- sub_sequence[left_idx] - sub_sequence[right_idx]
  
      if(delta < 0L) {
        delta <- delta * (-1L)
      }
      
      if(delta < 1L | delta > 3L) {
        jump_counter <- jump_counter + 1L
      }
    }
  
    # Check conditions
    if(rising_counter == len_sequence_1) rising <- 1L
    if(falling_counter == len_sequence_1) falling <- 1L
    if(jump_counter == 0L) no_jump <- 1L
    if(rising + falling + no_jump == 2L) out <- out + 1L
  }
  out
}

quick_check_sub_seq <- quick(check_sub_seq)
quick_check_all_sub_seq <- quick(check_all_sub_seq)

bench::mark(
  original = sum(unlist(map(sub_seq_list, org_check_sub_seq))),
  check_sub_seq = sum(unlist(map(sub_seq_list, check_sub_seq))),
  check_all_sub_seq = check_all_sub_seq(all_seq_vec, sub_seq_idx),
  quick_check_sub_seq = sum(unlist(map(sub_seq_list, quick_check_sub_seq))),
  quick_check_all_sub_seq = quick_check_all_sub_seq(all_seq_vec, sub_seq_idx)
)[1:7]

```
